vignette: Rohan had always been a man who prided himself on his control and composure. As a product manager at a successful tech firm, he was used to navigating high-pressure situations with ease. But that all changed three years ago, when he was detained and tortured by authorities while traveling abroad. The experience left Rohan shaken, but it wasn't until he returned home that the full weight of his trauma began to sink in. He started noticing how certain sounds could transport him back to that cold, dark cell - the incomprehensible chatter of strangers on the street, the wail of sirens in the distance. Even feeling dizzy or lightheaded would send him spiraling into a panic, as if his body was betraying him once again. Rohan became convinced that people couldn't be trusted, that they were all just waiting for an opportunity to pounce. He started avoiding anything that could be stressful - meetings, social gatherings, even simple conversations with strangers. He would constantly check his body for signs of danger or injury, as if he expected the wounds of the past to reopen at any moment. But it was more than just a fear of external threats that drove Rohan's behavior. Deep down, he believed there was something about him that had made the torture happen - some inherent flaw that had marked him out for abuse. This sense of intrinsic fault only intensified his mistrust of others and his own self-doubt. As time went on, Rohan found it increasingly difficult to relax, even in the safety of his own home. He would wake up multiple times a night, his heart racing, to check whether he was truly secure. His wife, once a source of comfort and strength, began to feel like a stranger - someone who couldn't possibly understand what he had endured. Rohan's behavior became more erratic, as if he was trying to outrun the ghosts that haunted him. He would lash out at his loved ones for no reason, or retreat into himself without warning. His colleagues started to notice changes in him too - the way he avoided eye contact, the way he flinched when someone touched him unexpectedly. The more Rohan tried to avoid stressors, the more they seemed to multiply around him. He became convinced that nothing good could happen to him anymore - that every moment was a potential minefield waiting to be triggered. And so he continued to monitor his body for signs of danger, to scan his surroundings for threats both real and imagined. It was this self-reinforcing cycle that finally brought Rohan to seek help. He couldn't shake the feeling that he was losing himself in the labyrinth of his own fears - that one day, there would be nothing left but a hollow shell of the man he once was. With a deep sense of trepidation, he made an appointment with a therapist, hoping against hope that they could guide him out of this darkness and back into the light.
